lesson.title: When Growth Control Fails: The Biology of Cancer
lesson.summary: Cancer results from the gradual accumulation of mutations that activate oncogenes and disable tumor suppressor genes, together disabling the checkpoints that normally keep cell division under control.
lesson.body:
Put the last several chapters together and a clear picture of cancer emerges: cancer is fundamentally a disease of cell cycle control. It does not arise from a single mutation but accumulates over years or decades, as a cell's descendants pick up mutation after mutation, some activating proto-oncogenes into oncogenes, others knocking out tumor suppressor genes, until the checkpoints that normally keep division in check stop working.

A normal cell with damaged DNA has three basic options, all enforced through the checkpoints already described: pause and repair, exit into G0, or, if the damage is severe, undergo apoptosis. A cell on its way to becoming cancerous has typically lost the ability to do any of these properly. With p53 or Rb disabled, checkpoint arrest fails. With apoptosis pathways impaired, damaged cells that should die instead survive. And with an oncogene like a mutated ras or an overactive cyclin gene supplying a constant, unregulated signal to divide, the cell no longer needs a real growth signal to keep cycling. The combination is what allows a single cell to become the founder of a growing, uncontrolled population, a tumor.

This is why cancer is often described as a multistep process, and colorectal cancer provides one of the most thoroughly documented examples. Many colorectal cancers begin with an early mutation in a tumor suppressor gene called APC, which allows a small benign growth, a polyp, to form. Later, a mutation activating the ras oncogene allows that polyp to grow larger and more abnormal. Finally, loss of p53 removes the last checkpoint controls, allowing the cells to become fully malignant, invading surrounding tissue and eventually spreading, or metastasizing, to distant sites in the body through the blood or lymphatic system. Each step in this sequence maps directly onto the concepts from the last few chapters: an oncogene supplying unwarranted go signals, and tumor suppressor genes failing to supply the corresponding stop signals.

It is also worth noting that genetic instability tends to compound the problem. Some tumor suppressor genes, including BRCA1, BRCA2, and components of the DNA damage response that normally work with p53, function specifically in detecting or repairing DNA damage. When these are lost, a cell not only loses a brake on division, it also loses its ability to fix new DNA errors accurately, which makes it more likely to accumulate the next mutation, and the next, at an accelerating rate. Cancer, in this sense, is not one broken part but a cascading failure of the entire quality control system that the cell cycle checkpoints, cyclins and CDKs, proto-oncogenes, and tumor suppressor genes together are built to maintain.
